HR@10 with one positive and 99 sampled negatives measures whether the positive reaches the top ten of that 100-item set. It does not estimate full-catalog HR@10 directly: sampled metrics can reverse model rankings even in expectation. Fixed candidates improve comparison reproducibility but do not remove sampling bias. Interpret gains as improvements under this specific benchmark protocol, without claiming better full-catalog retrieval. [Krichene & Rendle, 2020](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

For two fixed trained models, a practical adaptation of paired bootstrap resampling is to retain each user’s two hit indicators and resample users with replacement using identical indices for both models. Resample separately within each category, then recompute the equally weighted four-category mean difference; report the observed difference and a 95% bootstrap interval. With 200 users/category, one additional hit changes category HR by 0.5 percentage points and macro HR by 0.125 points. This interval describes user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the fitted models and observed candidate sets; it excludes training-seed variation and alternative negative draws. If the finite benchmark itself is the estimand, its measured difference is deterministic. [Paired-bootstrap foundation: Koehn, 2004](https://aclanthology.org/W04-3250/)

Repeatedly selecting checkpoints or architectures against the same validation users creates selection optimism, even when candidates and training seeds stay fixed. A bootstrap comparison performed after selecting the winner does not undo that adaptive selection. Treat small validation gains as exploratory; record how many alternatives were inspected, freeze the final selection, and reserve confirmatory claims for the host’s untouched held-out evaluation. [Cawley & Talbot, 2010](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)
